## Background

In this lab, I will be explroing the FiveThirtyEight's Halloween Candy dataset to figure out what is a top ranked candy during Halloween and exactly why!

## Import/Findings of Dataset

First, we will import the data and see what we are looking at!

```{r}
candy_file <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fivethirtyeight/data/master/candy-power-ranking/candy-data.csv"

candy = read.csv(candy_file, row.names=1)
head(candy)
```

> Q1. How many different candy types are in this dataset?

```{r}
nrow(candy)
```

> Q2. How many fruity candy types are in the dataset?

```{r}
sum(candy$fruity)
```

## What is Your Favorite Candy?

```{r}
candy["3 Musketeers", ]$winpercent
```

My favorite candy is 3 musketeers which ends up having a winpercent value of around 67.60%!

```{r}
candy["Kit Kat", ]$winpercent
```

> Q5. What is the winpercent value for “Tootsie Roll Snack Bars”?

```{r}
candy["Tootsie Roll Snack Bars", ]$winpercent
```

Before answering Q6-7, we must install and run the skim() package!

```{r}
library("skimr")
skim(candy)
```

> Q6. Is there any variable/column that looks to be on a different scale to the majority of the other columns in the dataset?

Yes, the winpercent looks the most different to the majority of other columns! While other columns including the different types of candy and the other percentages can be easily grouped together based on their similar shapes, winpercent is the only one with this unique shape.

> Q7. What do you think a zero and one represent for the candy\$chocolate column?

```{r}
candy$chocolate
```

For this column, the zero represents if the candy is missing the chocolate while the 1 represents the candy having chocolate!

## Exploratory Analysis

> Q8. Plot a histogram of winpercent values using both base R and ggplot2.

```{r}
hist(candy$winpercent,
     main = "Candy Win Percentages Distribution",
     xlab = "Win Percentage", 
     col = "lightpink")
```

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(candy, aes(x=winpercent)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, fill = "lightpink", color = "black")+   labs(title = "Candy Win Percentages Distribution",
                                                              x = "Win Percentage", 
                                                              y = "Number of Candies")
```

> Q9. Is the distribution of winpercent values symmetrical?

Based on both the plots, it is not symmetrical! It is more skewed on the right as most candies percentages ranged from 30-60%!

> Q10. Is the center of the distribution above or below 50%?

```{r}
mean(candy$winpercent)
median(candy$winpercent)
```

Based on the median as the center of distribution, it is slightly below 50% at 47.83%

> Q11. On average is chocolate candy higher or lower ranked than fruit candy?

```{r}
chocolate <- candy$winpercent[as.logical(candy$chocolate)]

fruit <- candy$winpercent[as.logical(candy$fruity)]

mean(chocolate)
mean(fruit)
```

On average, chocolate candies have a higher ranking than the fruit candies because it has an average of 60.92% while fruity candies is only 44.12%!

> Q12. Is this difference statistically significant?

```{r}
t.test(chocolate, fruit)
```

Because the p value is 2.871e-08, it is less than our known threshold value of 0.05! This concludes that this difference is statistically significant!

## Overall Candy Rankings

> Q13. What are the five least liked candy types in this set?

```{r}
head(candy[order(candy$winpercent), ], n=5)
```

> Q14. What are the top 5 all time favorite candy types out of this set?

```{r}
head(candy[order(candy$winpercent, decreasing=TRUE), ], n=5)
```

> Q15.Make a first barplot of candy ranking based on winpercent values.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(candy) + 
  aes(winpercent, rownames(candy)) +
  geom_col()
```

> Q16. This is quite ugly, use the reorder() function to get the bars sorted by winpercent?

```{r}
ggplot(candy) + 
  aes(winpercent, reorder(rownames(candy),winpercent))+
  geom_col()
```

Now that we have the graph, it's time to add some useful color!

Let's start by setting up a color vector that signifies candy type that we can use for future plots!

```{r}
my_cols=rep("black", nrow(candy))
my_cols[as.logical(candy$chocolate)] = "chocolate"
my_cols[as.logical(candy$bar)] = "brown"
my_cols[as.logical(candy$fruity)] = "pink"
```

Now create the plot!

```{r}
ggplot(candy) + 
  aes(winpercent, reorder(rownames(candy),winpercent)) +
  geom_col(fill=my_cols) +
  ylab("")
```

> Q17. What is the worst ranked chocolate candy?

The worst ranked chocolate is Sixlets!

> Q18. What is the best ranked fruity candy?

The best ranked fruity candy is Starburst!

## Taking a Look at Pricepercent

Now, we look at the prices of these candies and what is the best to get!

First, we will make a plot of winpercent vs pricepercent variables!

```{r}
library(ggrepel)

# How about a plot of win vs price
ggplot(candy) +
  aes(pricepercent, winpercent, label=rownames(candy)) +
  geom_point(col=my_cols) + 
  geom_text_repel(col=my_cols, size=3.3, max.overlaps = 5)
```

> Q19. Which candy type is the highest ranked in terms of winpercent for the least money - i.e. offers the most bang for your buck?

Based on the plot above, it seems as thought the Reese's Minatures are the best option! It's winpercent is around 81.87%, but its price percent is still low, equalng out to be less than 1%

> Q20. What are the top 5 most expensive candy types in the dataset and of these which is the least popular?

```{r}
ord <- order(candy$pricepercent, decreasing = TRUE)
head(candy[ord, c(11,12)], n=5)
```

Of the five most expensive using the code above, the least popular is Nik L Nip with a winpercent of 22.45%!

## Exploring the Correlation Structure

Now we look at the correlations between pairs and variables more closely!

```{r}
library(corrplot)
cij <- cor(candy)
corrplot(cij)
```

> Q22. Examining this plot what two variables are anti-correlated (i.e. have minus values)?

Examining this plot, two variables that are anti-correlated are chocolate and fruity !

> Q23. Use your corrplot result to make a prediction: which variables do you expect will have the largest contributions (i.e. loadings) to PC1 (i.e., drive the most separation between candies along the first principal component)?

The variables that I predict to have the alrgest contributions to PC1 would be chocolate and fruity because they are anti-correlated which helps in the long run when trying to separate the two groups and can help contribute to the variation in the dataset!

## PCA

Now let's apply PCA to our dataset!

```{r}
pca <- prcomp(candy, scale=TRUE)
summary(pca)
```

Time to plot our main PCA score plot of PC1 v PC2.

```{r}
plot(pca$x[, 1:2])
```

Add some color and change the plotting character!

```{r}
plot(pca$x[,1:2], col=my_cols, pch=16)
```

We can make an even nicer plot with the ggplot2 package!

```{r}
# Make a new data-frame with our PCA results and candy data
my_data <- cbind(candy, pca$x[,1:3])
```

```{r}
p <- ggplot(my_data) + 
        aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, 
            size=winpercent/100,  
            text=rownames(my_data),
            label=rownames(my_data)) +
        geom_point(col=my_cols)

p
```

Test it out with the ggrepel package!

```{r}
library(ggrepel)

p + geom_text_repel(size=3.3, col=my_cols, max.overlaps = 7)  + 
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(title="Halloween Candy PCA Space",
       subtitle="Colored by type: chocolate bar (dark brown), chocolate other (light brown), fruity (red), other (black)",
       caption="Data from 538")
```

Let's finish by taking a look at our PCA loadings!

> Q24. Complete the code to generate the loadings plot above. What original variables are picked up strongly by PC1 in the positive direction? Do these make sense to you? Where did you see this relationship highlighted previously?

```{r}
ggplot(pca$rotation) +
  aes(PC1, reorder(rownames(pca$rotation), PC1)) +
  geom_col()
```

In positive direction, the variables that conitrbution are fruity, pluribus, and sugarpercent which makes sense because fruity candy are more likely to not contain anything choclate related (which reflects in the characteristics)l. Moreover, we saw this when we found the anti-correlation between fruity and chocolate candies!

## Summary

> Q25. Based on your exploratory analysis, correlation findings, and PCA results, what combination of characteristics appears to make a “winning” candy? How do these different analyses (visualization, correlation, PCA) support or complement each other in reaching this conclusion?

Based on my exploratory analysis, I think a winning candy should consist of being a chocolate with nuts such as almonds/peanuts and usually in a bar shaped! Chocolates overall had a higher winpercent compared to any other (including fruity). We saw that when we compared the two percentages side by side with chocolate having 60.92% while 44.12% was fruity! This was further supported when we saw more positive correlations for chocolate, bar, and even their different popularity and price points! The PCA was able to confirm everything because it should that bar, choclate, winpercent, and pricepercent were all in the same direction while the fruit was in the completely opposite direction. Moreover, the different point sizes in all the comparison PCA plots indicated that chocolates and winpercent were clearly more correlated with each other!
